title: How can a user script map its own DOM node object to the page’s?
body_excerpt: User scripts are typically executed in a separate realm from the page on which they run, and the objects that represent DOM nodes in the user script are not the same objects that the actual page accesses . And that, for the most part, is a good thing: it prevents mutations to properties and prototypes performed by the page from affecting (and therefore potentially breaking) the user script. But occasionally, a user script needs to pierce through that sandbox and obtain the page’s DOM node object, because the one the user script normally uses lacks some extra properties that the page has installed on its own DOM node object. title: Detect use of HTTP2/3 in javascript
body_excerpt: Actual problem The actual problem I'm trying to solve is loading resources, among which are potentially 8+ ( more than the parallel connection limit ) long-running requests. (nd-json) The issue is that some firewalls block HTTP2 and HTTP3, so clients automatically fall back to HTTP1. Given parallel connection limits, this can put some fetch requests on hold indefinitely, if the long-running requests fire first. The workaround is to have a number of aliased domains that requests are round-robin'ed between, but this breaks most of the performance advantages of HTTP2&3, which brings me to my question. (if anyone has an idea for a workaround that doesn't have this issue, I'd be happy to hear it) Detecting HTTP 1.1 vs 2 or 3 Older questions have answers relating to performance APIs, but as far as I can see, those have been deprecated, replaced, or shielded for privacy reasons. Also suggested is having the server tell the client which protocol it used. This works in the simple case, but with load balancers and other possible intermediate infrastructure, there might be a mismatch between the protocol the client speaks, and the one the server speaks. A stupidly simple solution might be to first attempt 10 simultaneous long-running requests, then do a simple request with a timeout, and fall back to round-robin if that doesn't get served, but that feels very hacky.

title: Prisma throws "No database host or connection string was set" despite environment variables being configured
body_excerpt: I'm getting the following error on my Next.js app (deployed on Vercel) when navigating to the "Add Your Store" page, which triggers a database operation via Prisma: ``` No database host or connection string was set, and key parameters have default values (host: localhost, user: undefined, db: undefined, password: null). Is an environment variable missing? Alternatively, if you intended to connect with these parameters, please set the host to 'localhost' explicitly. ``` **Stack:** - Next.js (App Router) - Prisma ORM - Neon PostgreSQL (serverless) - Deployed on Vercel **What I've done:** - Set `DATABASE_URL` in Vercel environment variables (using the pooler connection string from Neon) - Set `DATABASE_URL_UNPOOLED` separately for migrations - Ran `prisma migrate deploy` as part of the build command **What I've checked:** - The env variables are defined in Vercel's dashboard under the correct environment (Production/Preview) - `schema.prisma` references `env("DATABASE_URL")` - The error suggests the variable is not being picked up at runtime (`user: undefined`, `db: undefined`) **Question:** Why is Prisma not reading the `DATABASE_URL` at runtime on Vercel, and what's the correct way to ensure the connection string is available to Prisma in a serverless Next.js deployment with Neon PostgreSQL?
